meetings.route: TIE 24H business or short business entry

meetings.next: Ask the host whether Re.N.U.R.E. registration and TIE 24H are needed.

conference.detail: Attendance can fit visitor/business purpose; professional delivery and paid tasks are separately named in TIE categories.
conference.next: Label attendee, speaker, trainer and exhibitor roles.
conference.basis: From Luke's earlier notes; not yet verified against an official source.

unpaid-speaking.detail: The electronic-entry menu expressly lists remunerated or non-remunerated scientific, professional, technical, religious or artistic tasks.

unpaid-speaking.basis: From Luke's earlier notes; not yet verified against an official source.

paid-speaking.route: TIE 24H or temporary residence for local professional work
paid-speaking.detail: Argentina's migration categories can cover paid professional/technical/artistic tasks, but a proper permission is not the same as tourist entry.
paid-speaking.next: Have the registered requester choose the short TIE or temporary-residence category.
paid-speaking.basis: From Luke's earlier notes; not yet verified against an official source.

book-launch.detail: Rights meetings can be business; paid readings, workshops, signings, royalties and local sales should use the professional/artistic and tax framework.

ai-teaching.route: Scientific/professional TIE or academic host route
ai-teaching.detail: Short teaching can be tied to a university or professional invitation; recurring local employment needs residence/work status.

ai-teaching.basis: From Luke's earlier notes; not yet verified against an official source.

remote-work.route: Digital-nomad category listed in TIE 24H system
remote-work.detail: Argentina's electronic-entry menu includes digital nomads; current duration, evidence and whether a visa is needed must be confirmed for the passport and stay.

entrepreneur.detail: Founder and investor activity is a residence/company question; the visitor/business route only supports exploration and meetings.

trade.route: Business/TIE route; local import and fulfilment separate

laws.rule: If you plan to take part in commercial or altruistic surrogacy arrangements in Argentina, be aware of all legal and other risks involved. Research prospective agencies and clinics to ensure that you're dealing with a reputable organisation. Get comprehensive and independent legal advice from an Argentine lawyer with specialisation in this area of law. There's no specific legislation that regulates surrogacy and all surrogacy arrangements are subject to ongoing developments in Argentine law. This applies to both the surrogacy arrangements as well as administrative procedures such as issuing of birth certificates and travel arrangements for babies born through surrogacy. Argentine authorities

laws.rule: On arrival in Argentina, declare cash or monetary instruments (in any currency) worth US$10,000 or more; for travellers under 16 the figure is US$5,000. Goods regulated by SENASA (the national food and animal and plant health service) must also be declared. US$10,000 is about A$14,200 (RBA 30 Oct 2026: A$1 = USD 0.7040).

Goods bought abroad up to US$500 (air or sea arrival) can come in without tax; for land or river arrival there is no allowance except Puerto Iguazu (US$500). Above the limit, you pay half of the value over it (for example, on goods worth US$600 you pay US$50).

money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: The Peso (ARS) is the official currency of Argentina. Most major hotels in Buenos Aires will exchange US dollars. Check local sources for advice on buying foreign currency. Don't exchange money on the street, or with someone offering exchange services on the street. You may receive counterfeit pesos or become the victim of a crime. Credit/debit cards are widely accepted. You should carry a photocopy of the identity page of your passport or a photo ID in case you are required to prove you are the owner of the card. Ask your bank in Australia if your ATM card will work and if it has an affiliate

closures: official: Argentina 2027 national holidays, dates worked out from Ley 27.399 (https://servicios.infoleg.gob.ar/infolegInternet/anexos/280000-284999/281835/norma.htm); no 2027 decree has been read, so this is computed from the statute. Fixed: Fri 1 Jan; Wed 24 Mar; Fri 2 Apr; Sat 1 May; Tue 25 May; Sun 20 Jun; Fri 9 Jul; Wed 8 Dec; Sat 25 Dec. Movable under article 6 (Tuesday or Wednesday moves to the previous Monday, Thursday or Friday to the next Monday): 17 Jun (Thu) moves to Mon 21 Jun; 17 Aug (Tue) moves to Mon 16 Aug; 12 Oct (Tue) moves to Mon 11 Oct; 20 Nov falls on a Saturday and article 6 does not say it moves. Carnival Monday and Tuesday and Good Friday follow Easter and are not given here. The executive can add up to three tourism bridge days a year by decree; none for 2027 has been read.

drone-pilot-pathway.summary: ANAC accepts a foreign remote pilot licence for that class of aircraft if apostilled and translated into Spanish; without one, a visitor is limited to Class A recreational drones, though ANAC can grant a temporary exceptional authorisation for isolated commercial work. ANAC has recently simplified commercial rules; the current exact text was not confirmed.

items.text: Not yet checked: no public ANAC directory of drone operators was found on the pages read.

Non-recreational drones are registered with ANAC. Remote pilots hold a Certificate of Competence (VANT/SVANT). An official ANAC news item says unnecessary approvals for commercial operations were removed and the operator now designates suitable pilots; the exact current rule was not confirmed.

A foreign remote pilot with a licence from their own country for that type of aircraft does not need the Argentine certificate if the licence is apostilled and translated into Spanish. Otherwise they obtain the Argentine certificate or fly only Class A recreational drones. ANAC may grant a temporary, exceptional authorisation for isolated, non-habitual scientific, commercial or sports operations.
